name: libsoxr (SoX Resampler library)
baseline: libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code) 'sinc_best' through the Python 'samplerate' and 'scikits.samplerate' wrappers
workload: Resample a 2 s, 96,000-sample float64 mono log-sweep from 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz in Python with %timeit; soxr measured through the python-soxr binding with default settings.
claimed_speedup: soxr.resample 1.16 ms +/- 2.42 us per call versus samplerate sinc_best 76.8 ms +/- 1.03 ms and scikits.samplerate sinc_best 75.5 ms +/- 57.4 us, about 66x faster than samplerate (derived from page data). The same shootout lists scipy.signal.resample 2.42 ms, torchaudio 9.98-10 ms, resampy kaiser_fast 10.5 ms, resampy kaiser_best 44.8 ms, nnresample 16 ms, julius 16.2 ms.
stars_or_usage: 181 stars; widely packaged and bound from Python
tradeoffs: LGPL licence, a copyleft constraint for static linking. Throughput comes from large internal batches, so latency is high (the SampleRateTap comparison measures 8.8-16.4 ms for soxr HQ).
caveats: Independent third-party shootout (jonashaag/audio-resampling-in-python, last commit 2021-06-09) found as extra evidence for an already catalogued project. It measures the python-soxr and python-samplerate wrappers, not the C libraries directly; the notebook was run in a Colab-style environment with no CPU model stated, and quality settings are not matched (soxr defaults versus libsamplerate sinc_best, the slowest and highest-quality converter), so the ratio overstates a like-for-like gap. libsoxr's own repo has no commits since 2018-02-24.
found_via: WebSearch 'audio resampler benchmark libsamplerate soxr speexdsp zita-resampler comparison speed github repository results table'

name: libsoxr (SoX Resampler library)
workload: Time to convert generated RightMark test files (44.1, 48 and 96 kHz stereo, 16-bit integer or 32-bit float) to other rates with the speex and soxr command-line test harness, all files on tmpfs, real/user/system seconds.
claimed_speedup: Real seconds, 44.1 kHz 16-bit to 48 kHz: speex-10 4.35, speex-5 0.56, speex-1 0.23 versus soxr-vhq 0.29, soxr-hq 0.16, soxr-mq 0.15, soxr-lq 0.23. 48 kHz 16-bit to 44.1 kHz: speex-10 4.32, speex-5 0.52 versus soxr-vhq 0.25, soxr-hq 0.19. 96 kHz float to 44.1 kHz: speex-10 5.43 versus soxr-vhq 0.30. Top presets therefore about 15-18x faster (derived from page data); speex-5 versus soxr-hq about 2.7-3.5x (derived).
hardware: Core i7 2600K with 16 GiB RAM, Kubuntu 14.10 x86_64, soxr 0.1.1
tradeoffs: LGPL licence. soxr's quality presets add input delay of about 20 ms at HQ/VHQ in this page's delay table versus 0.17-2.9 ms for speex presets, so it suits offline or buffered conversion more than ultra-low-latency use.
caveats: Independent third-party comparison (Lastique/src_test, code and results published; last commit 2022-04-15), found as extra evidence for an already catalogued project. The data is from 2014 (soxr 0.1.1, speex 1.2rc1) so both libraries have moved on; compiler and flags are not stated; quality is compared by spectrograms, not matched quantitatively, so pairing speex-10 with soxr-vhq is approximate. The page's results are single runs per cell with no variance. libsoxr's own repo has no commits since 2018-02-24.
found_via: WebSearch 'audio resampler benchmark libsamplerate soxr speexdsp zita-resampler comparison speed github repository results table' (page lastique.github.io/src_test read via its gh-pages branch on raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: Wuffs (std/png and std/gif decoders)
workload: 'wuffs bench -mimic' decode throughput on PNG (19k to 4002k-byte decoded images) and GIF (1k to 1000k-pixel images and an animated screencap) against the mimic libraries as shipped with Debian Bullseye, measured as of September 2022.
claimed_speedup: PNG decode versus libpng 1.00x: gcc10 2.27x, 2.33x, 2.70x, 3.01x (552k verify_checksum), 1.65x (4002k 24bpp); clang11 1.55x to 2.90x; libspng 0.7.3 sits at 1.02x to 1.36x of libpng, lodepng 0.77x to 1.13x, stb 0.76x to 1.23x. GIF decode versus libgif: 1.92x to 6.58x (gcc10) and 1.96x to 6.58x (clang11), for example 1.31 GB/s versus 199 MB/s on the animated screencap.
compiler_and_flags: clang 11.0.1 and gcc 10.2.1; reproduction recipe 'gcc -O3 test/c/std/zlib.c' then './a.out -bench', 'wuffs bench -mimic std/png'; mimic libraries as shipped by Debian Bullseye (libpng 1.6.37, libgif 5.1.9, zlib 1.2.11)
tradeoffs: PNG and GIF decoders only (no PNG encoder in the standard library); generated single-file C is usable from C and C++ but regenerating needs the Go-based Wuffs toolchain. Memory-safe by construction.
caveats: Numbers date from September 2022 with Debian's libpng 1.6.37, zlib 1.2.11 and gcc 10 / clang 11, so newer libpng or zlib-ng builds may narrow the gap. libpng's simplified API cannot skip the checksum, so its verify_checksum number is reused as the 1.00x baseline. Small-image deflate decode is slower than zlib (0.76x to 0.93x at 1k). The project's own benchmark, not an independent run, although the QOIR and jpeg-nitro READMEs also measure it against other decoders.
found_via: Opened google/wuffs doc/benchmarks.md (the shootout the task named) and nigeltao.github.io blog markdown for the PNG decoder appendix

name: QOIR (independent run in Image-Compression-Benchmark)
workload: Total compress and decompress time on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB), single-threaded, QOIR.exe against Pillow PNG.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: QOIR 23.696 s compress, 19.752 s decompress, 2,139,350,533 bytes versus PNG 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes (about 14x and 1.7x faster, 6.8% larger, derived). GDCC2020: QOIR 5.274 s and 4.323 s versus PNG 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 29x and 2.7x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Experimental format subject to incompatible changes; single-file C library; files are larger than PNG (6.8% on CLIC2021, 22% on GDCC2020 by the numbers above).
caveats: Third-party run on different hardware from the QOIR README (Windows prebuilt executable, i7-12700H), so flags are unknown and the grade is B. Baseline is Pillow's PNG codec, not libpng, and includes Python process effects. On the small Kodak set the gap shrinks to start-up noise (PNG optimize=False decodes 0.484 s versus QOIR 0.640 s).
found_via: Image-Compression-Benchmark README (WangXuan95), independent confirmation of the QOIR claim

name: Zpng (independent run in Image-Compression-Benchmark)
workload: Total compress and decompress time on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB), single-threaded, ZPNG.exe default mode (-c) and -19.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: ZPNG 25.909 s compress, 24.083 s decompress, 1,755,786,378 bytes versus PNG 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes (about 12.9x and 1.4x faster, 12% smaller, derived); ZPNG -19 decompresses in 20.486 s (about 1.6x) at 1,703,197,687 bytes but compresses in 1529.037 s. GDCC2020: ZPNG 5.415 s and 5.415 s versus PNG 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 28x and 2.1x) at about the same size (522,105,496 versus 521,104,646 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Experimental format, not PNG-compatible; about 500 to 700 lines plus a dependency on zstd.
caveats: Third-party run with prebuilt executables (flags unknown, grade B); baseline is Pillow's zlib-based PNG codec, not libpng. On photographic data ZPNG wins on size too, but on GDCC2020 the sizes are even. Repository last touched in 2018.
found_via: Image-Compression-Benchmark README (WangXuan95), independent confirmation of the Zpng claim

name: QOI (independent run in Image-Compression-Benchmark)
workload: Total compress and decompress time on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB), single-threaded, QOI via ImCvt.exe.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: QOI 19.061 s compress, 18.970 s decompress, 2,280,217,586 bytes versus PNG 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes (about 17.6x and 1.8x faster, 13.8% larger, derived). GDCC2020: QOI 4.782 s and 4.174 s versus PNG 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 32x and 2.8x, derived), at 711,448,440 versus 521,104,646 bytes (36% larger).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Files are noticeably larger than PNG (14% to 36% in these runs); the benchmark lists QOI as RGB 24-bit only (no gray 8-bit).
caveats: Third-party run through a converter executable (ImCvt.exe) with unknown flags; baseline is Pillow's PNG codec, not libpng, and the speed gap is mostly encode speed. On small Kodak images decoding is slower than PNG optimize=False (0.638 s versus 0.484 s).
found_via: Image-Compression-Benchmark README (WangXuan95), independent confirmation of the QOI claim

name: Blend2D (vello_chart shootout aggregate)
workload: bl_bench-style suite in LaurenzV/vello_chart: 29 fill/stroke shape tests x six paint styles (solid, linear, radial, conic, two image-pattern filters) x six sizes (8x8 to 256x256), SrcOver, 512x600 prgb32 target, render calls per ms; Blend2D 0.12.0 single-threaded and 2, 4, 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, geometric mean over all test/size cells (derived from page data): single thread 4.08x Skia (faster in 99% of 1044 cells; 2.52x at 8x8 rising to 5.61x at 256x256) and 7.11x Cairo (99% of 870 cells); 8 threads 11.45x Skia and 20.55x Cairo (8 threads 2.81x its own single thread). Intel i9-14900K Windows run: 6.13x Cairo (no Skia there).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release per the harness README; compiler and flags not stated in the result data
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS); second dataset Intel Core i9-14900K (x86_64, Windows)
tradeoffs: Uses a JIT (AsmJit) pipeline generator; C++ library with its own text, image codecs and stroker.
caveats: Extra independent-style evidence for the already known Blend2D entry (same thesis data as the papers entry, but aggregated over the full result file). Harness is a LaurenzV fork of the Blend2D bl_bench tool (github.com/LaurenzV/blend2d-apps, with Skia, JUCE, AGG and Cairo backends; CMake Release build); compiler, compiler version and flags are not stated in the result files, hence tier B not A. The runner is the author of Vello CPU and the harness comes from the Blend2D author, so neither is neutral for these two libraries; the Skia version is not recorded in the data. Data used Blend2D 0.12.0 while the repo is at v0.21.3, so current speed may differ.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/LaurenzV/vello_chart data/manifest.json and data/arm/2026-06-08.json, linked from the LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf

name: Vello CPU (vello_chart shootout aggregate)
workload: Same bl_bench-style suite as the Blend2D aggregate entry (29 tests x six paint styles x six sizes, 512x600 target, render calls per ms) with vello_cpu through the LaurenzV/vello_cpu_c C bindings; single thread and 2, 4, 8 threads.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, geometric mean over all test/size cells (derived from page data): single thread 2.50x Skia (faster in 91% of 1044 cells; 1.59x at 8x8 rising to 3.42x at 256x256) and 4.33x Cairo (94% of 870 cells); 8 threads 7.54x Skia and 12.55x Cairo (3.02x its own single thread). Intel i9-14900K Windows run: 2.75x Cairo. Slower than Blend2D single-threaded (0.61x on M1 Pro, 0.43x on i9, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86, default NEON on ARM (thesis Section 5.2); C++ harness CMake Release; compiler versions not stated
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS); second dataset Intel Core i9-14900K (x86_64, Windows)
stars_or_usage: 4.4k stars (linebender/vello, which also holds the GPU renderer)
tradeoffs: Rust crate (needs the C bindings or Rust FFI from C++); sparse-strips architecture with SIMD and optional multithreading; also has a hybrid CPU/GPU variant.
caveats: Extra evidence for the already known Vello CPU entry. Harness is a LaurenzV fork of the Blend2D bl_bench tool (github.com/LaurenzV/blend2d-apps, with Skia, JUCE, AGG and Cairo backends; CMake Release build); compiler, compiler version and flags are not stated in the result files, hence tier B not A. The runner is the author of Vello CPU and the harness comes from the Blend2D author, so neither is neutral for these two libraries; the Skia version is not recorded in the data. The vello_chart data is run by the Vello CPU author (LaurenzV), who also wrote the thesis, so this is not a neutral third-party measurement for Vello CPU; the repo page now lists vello_cpu as a top-level vello_cpu/ directory (the thesis footnote points to sparse_strips/vello_cpu).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): github.com/LaurenzV/vello_chart data/arm/2026-06-08.json, linked from the LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf

name: Pillow-SIMD
workload: libvips benchmark pipeline (crop, 10 percent bilinear shrink, 3x3 sharpen on a 10000x10000 TIFF); pillow-perf resize of 2560x1600 RGB, colour conversion, 3D LUT and blur.
claimed_speedup: libvips wiki: pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s vs magick 4.41 s and convert 4.44 s (2.9x, derived from page data) on a 16-core machine although Pillow is single-threaded. pillow-perf on Core i5-4430 (derived from page data): Lanczos 2560x1600 to 320x200 6.09 ms (Pillow SIMD 7.0.0 AVX2) vs ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 134.41 ms (22x) and plain Pillow 7.0.0 40.46 ms; bilinear 2.40 vs 47.76 ms (20x); RGB to L 2.17 vs 51.45 ms (24x); 3D LUT 4^3 table 14.59 vs 3353.63 ms (230x). Xeon E5-2666 v3, Pillow SIMD 3.4.0 AVX2 Lanczos 320x200 7.38 ms vs Skia 53 18.1 ms vs ImageMagick 6.8.9-9 127.67 ms.
compiler_and_flags: pillow-perf labels builds '-msse4' and '-mavx2'; compiler version not stated; libvips wiki used the pip package.
hardware: libvips wiki: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04. pillow-perf: Core i5-4430, Xeon 8124M, EPYC 7571, Core i5-8279U, Xeon E5-2666 v3.
tradeoffs: Python extension only; on AMD EPYC 7571 the AVX2 build is no faster than SSE4 (pillow-perf notes 128-bit execution units).
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project: the libvips table is an independent third-party suite (hardware stated, no flags). pillow-perf is run by the Pillow-SIMD authors, and the ImageMagick versions there are old.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use table and pillow-perf docs/src/data/*.json.

name: libvips
workload: pillow-perf: JPEG load/save and a full load/transpose/resize/blur cycle on a 2560x1600 image; speedtest-resize: load a 5616x3744 JPEG, make a 150x100 thumbnail, save.
claimed_speedup: pillow-perf full cycle on Core i5-4430 (vips 8.9 vs ImageMagick 6.9.7-4, cumulative): 102.14 ms vs 328.75 ms (3.2x, derived from page data); JPEG save 36.21 vs 48.04 ms; JPEG load 25.18 vs 27.38 ms. speedtest-resize, Pentium T2390 scenario: vipsthumbnail 0.120 s vs ImageMagick_resize 2.316 s (19x, derived) and ImageMagick_thumbnail 0.326 s; Core i7 3.4GHz scenario: vipsthumbnail 0.115 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (4.9x, derived), vips 0.070 s, but ImageMagick_thumbnail 0.057 s is faster than vips in that scenario.
hardware: speedtest-resize: Intel Pentium Dual T2390 @ 1.86GHz Ubuntu 14.04, and Intel Core i7 3.4GHz Ubuntu 16.10; pillow-perf: Core i5-4430 @ 3.00GHz Ubuntu 18.04.3
stars_or_usage: 11.7k stars; used by Mastodon, Rails and imgproxy per its README
tradeoffs: Fastest on large images and with JPEG shrink-on-load; for very small PNGs libvips was slower and heavier than ImageMagick in a user report (libvips issue 3654: 0.41 s and 10.6 MB vs 0.10 s and 10 MB for a 500KB PNG to 64x64).
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project. Third-party numbers show the ImageMagick thumbnail mode with a jpeg:size hint matching or beating libvips on one machine. The pillow-perf suite is by the Pillow-SIMD authors. In libvips discussion 4710 (user-run, hardware not captured) libvips took 2.133 s for 100 6000x4000 JPEGs vs GraphicsMagick 2.015 s and ImageMagick 2.325 s, because libjpeg dominates; the maintainer notes the advantage appears on larger images and multi-operation pipelines.
found_via: github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize README, pillow-perf data files, libvips issue 3654 and libvips discussion 4710.

name: GraphicsMagick
baseline: ImageMagick (npm 'imagemagick' CLI wrapper in the sharp benchmark; ImageMagick resize and thumbnail commands in speedtest-resize)
workload: sharp benchmark: decompress a 2725x2225 JPEG, resize to 720x588 with Lanczos 3, compress to JPEG at quality 80; also a 2048x1536 RGBA PNG resized to 720x540 with premultiply and PNG output.
claimed_speedup: sharp docs, ops/sec (derived ratios from page data): AMD64 JPEG gm 21.04 vs imagemagick 16.23 (1.3x), PNG gm 13.35 vs imagemagick 10.37 (1.3x); ARM64 JPEG gm 13.72 vs imagemagick 5.85 (2.3x), PNG gm 9.45 vs imagemagick 4.39 (2.2x). speedtest-resize (Core i7 3.4GHz): GraphicsMagick_thumbnail 0.172 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s, but ImageMagick_thumbnail takes 0.057 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (packaged binaries driven from Node.js 24.15.0 on Ubuntu 25.10).
hardware: AWS EC2 c8a.xlarge (4x AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.xlarge (4x ARM Graviton4)
tradeoffs: Same command-line style as ImageMagick with a smaller feature set; the sharp suite shells out to the gm binary.
caveats: Evidence record for an already-catalogued project (see its libvips-wiki entry). The sharp benchmark is run by the sharp author, so it is third party for GraphicsMagick; the speedtest-resize author was surprised that GraphicsMagick was slower than ImageMagick in his scenario, so the sign of the result depends on the ImageMagick command used. In libvips discussion 4710 GraphicsMagick (2.015 s) also beat ImageMagick 6 (2.325 s, 1.15x) on 100 JPEGs.
found_via: sharp performance docs (contenders imagemagick, gm, jimp) and github.com/fawick/speedtest-resize README.
